bearings.paper_claim: Neuroticism goes with more negative-emotion words, fewer positive-emotion words and more first-person singular. Big Five self-report correlations with word use are r = 0.10 to 0.16 in several hundred college students (Pennebaker and King 1999). Depressed students (Rude et al. 2002) used more I, with me, my and mine comparable. Emotion words are under 5 percent of words in speech, writing and poetry.

bearings.paper_claim: Word use is consistent across text types for 36 LIWC dimensions (Pennebaker and King 1999). Four-week retest of student everyday conversation (EAR, 52 college students, Mehl and Pennebaker 2002a) was r = 0.41 for standard linguistic variables and 0.24 for psychological-process variables. Successive 2-minute speech intervals correlated 0.51 across 21 categories, a result the review attributes to Gleser et al. 1959 on 5-minute talks.
bearings.paper_location: Psychometric Properties of Word Use pp. 555-556; 52 college students p. 557.

Floor, press and social text is outside its scope. The inference that 0.24 retest reliability predicts weak genre transfer is the analyst's, not the paper's.

bearings.paper_claim: Emotion words are under 5 percent of words in daily speech, emotional writing and affect-laden poetry, so emotion-word counts predict emotional state weakly. Word-count programs cannot consider context, irony or sarcasm. In at least two studies, judges' ratings of emotionality correlated more highly with language use than with self-reports.

summary_issues: The successive 2-minute r = 0.51 is from Gleser et al. 1959 on 5-minute talks, not the review own data. The summary should attribute it.
The 0.41 and 0.24 retest figures are Mehl and Pennebaker 2002a EAR data from 52 college students. The summary should attribute them.
Judge sentence: the summary says judges agree with its language more closely. The paper says ratings correlated more highly with language than with self-reports, in at least two studies.

Evidence source: the summary says US college students. The review mixes student self-reports, diaries, journal abstracts, poets, elderly depressed speakers and chat-room dyads, and states no country for these samples.
Depression: the I-only effect comes from student personal essays (Rude et al. 2002), not a clinical sample. The summary omits the sample.

The mean held-out r of .350 against RKH, and the claim the literature cannot support it, are analyst comparisons across different measures, not paper findings. The .350 figure was not located in the fec/members code or docs searched.
The claim that low reliability of psychological-process categories makes failed cross-genre transfers unsurprising is an inference. The review does not discuss genre transfer.
Function-word gap: the review names particles as a research priority and I-to-we as a shared-upheaval signal. It does not call them the most informative signal.
Shared-upheaval figures (135 percent, 12 percent, back to normal by day 10) come from one online chat-room study after Princess Diana death (Stone and Pennebaker 2002), not a general pattern.
Ghost-writing and authorship are not discussed in the review. That gap is the analyst's, not paper content.
Page errors: the Big Five passage is p. 558, not 559; the judges passage is p. 559 under Traditional Personality Measures, not Summary p. 560.
